 Republican Senate leader Chris Garten asks Indiana Supreme Court to let him take office
 By 
 Tom Davies 
 - 
 November 17, 2026 11:11 am 
 Sen. Chris Garten, R-Charlestown, speaks during a February 2026 Senate session. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
 Attorneys for Republican state Sen. Chris Garten have asked the Indiana Supreme Court to throw out a judge’s order blocking him from taking the oath of office Tuesday with other newly elected legislators. 
 The court filings come just hours before the Senate’s Organization Day session scheduled for 1:30 p.m. Tuesday, when the majority Republicans planned to install him in the chamber’s top position of president pro tem . 
 Garten’s attorneys argue that Scott County Circuit Court Judge Jason Mount exceeded his authority by issuing a temporary restraining order Monday preventing Garten from “presenting himself to take the oath of office as, or to be seated as, the Senator from District 45.” 
 The Supreme Court did not make any immediate rulings Tuesday morning. 
 The restraining order sought by the Clark County Democratic chairman argued that voting equipment problems on Election Day in Jeffersonville leave questions about the accuracy of the reported election results. 
 Judge issues order blocking Indiana Senate GOP leader Chris Garten from starting new term 
 The tallies for Senate District 45 — which includes all of Clark County and a portion of Floyd County — show Garten ahead of Democratic challenger Nick Marshall by 297 votes, or about two-thirds of a percentage point. 
 Garten’s attorneys argue that the state constitution gives each house of the Legislature the exclusive authority to determine “the elections, qualifications, and returns of its own members.” 
 “The order stops the certification the recount statutes assume, and it purports to forbid a Senator-elect from presenting himself to the Senate,” they say in a court filing. “That is a court impermissibly deciding who may be heard by the Senate on its organizing day.” 
 Garten is represented by prominent conservative attorney James Bopp, along with Ted Nolting and Philip Lashutka of the Indianapolis firm Kroger, Gardis and Regas. 
 Democrats argued that Garten should not be allowed to be sworn in for a new four-year term before the Indiana Recount Commission can review the race. 
 Democrats maintain the Clark County Election Board — controlled 2-1 by Republicans — failed to adequately review problems involving four precincts that voted at Jeffersonville High School, where a ballot scanner malfunction was reported on Election Day. 
 Mount, a Democrat, was assigned as the special judge after a Clark County judge’s recusal from the case, according to court records. Mount is the brother of Republican U.S. Rep. Erin Houchin, who served in the state Senate with Garten. 
 Democrats have said they intend to seek a recount of the Senate race results. Candidates have until Tuesday to file recount petitions, with county party chairs having a Friday deadline. 
 Garten’s attorneys argue that state law lays out a recount as the proper process that should be followed. 
 “A recount and contest before the Recount Commission is the remedy the General Assembly created for the claims Petitioner raises,” they said in court filings. 
 State law says the Recount Commission must complete a legislative recount by December 20, unless it extends the deadline for good cause.
